newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz vows allegiance to secularism.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz vows allegiance to secularism.

text.p: Turkey's new Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz pledged his allegiance to the country's secularist traditions on Sunday, a day after a confidence vote victory applauded by the anti-Islamist media.
Parliament voted by a clear margin on Saturday to approve a two-week-old coalition under Yilmaz that is designed to keep the Islam-based Welfare Party from returning to power.
Conservative Yilmaz, accompanied by cabinet ministers in his right-left coalition, placed a wreath at the tomb of Turkey's secularist founder Mustafa Kemal Ataturk in a traditional sign of respect.
"The republic, which you described as 'my greatest work', is in safe hands. You can sleep peacefully," Yilmaz wrote in a book of condolences as political leaders looked on.

"We are aware of our responsibility to work towards preserving your immutable principles and reaching a level of modern civilisation," Yilmaz wrote in a ceremony at the imposing mausoleum on a hill overlooking the Turkish capital.

The mainstream secularist media applauded the new coalition, which faces the task of reuniting a country riven by religious and political divisions after a year under the country's first Islamist leader, Necmettin Erbakan.
"Congratulations. Parliament produced a 'democratic solution,'" a headline in the liberal Yeni Yuzyil daily said of the government's confidence vote win by 281 to 256 votes.
"A new age. The Islamist-led government, which strained Turkey for a year, is consigned to history," said the mass circulation Sabah newspaper.

The new government has vowed to reassert Turkey's bid for greater integration with Europe after a year in which Welfare leader Erbakan sought to strengthen the secular, Moslem nation's links with the Islamic world.

Erbakan protested at the formation of the alliance under Yilmaz, which arose from President Suleyman Demirel's decision to reject a planned transfer of power within the Islamist-led coalition in June.

"The country was brought to this point by force. The people did not bring this about. The people will not be responsible for the ensuing destruction," Erbakan was quoted by Anatolian news agency as telling a party meeting.
Yilmaz promised to restrict Islamic education -- one of the most sensitive issues in the battle for the country's hearts and minds -- in the government programme announced last week.
Deputy Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit said the coalition aimed to delay parliament's summer break to introduce a law increasing state education to eight years from five.
"We definitely want to produce a law on eight-year education before the holiday so that it can be applied during the school year ahead of us," he told reporters, according to Anatolian.
An Islamist MP attacked the anti-Islamist line of the new government and called for early elections.

"Mr Yilmaz, you cannot go on with such a ragtag government. Political morality and the national will have been deeply wounded," Welfare deputy Remzi Cetin wrote in the party's official newspaper. "You must urgently seek elections."
The last months of Erbakan's tenure were marred by fierce public debate over Islam, democracy and the right of the influential army to play politics.
Yilmaz has previously vowed to seek early elections, but made no mention of polls in the government programme. Elections are not due until the year 2000.
Factional timebombs within his alliance, the enduring power in parliament of the Islamists and Turkey's deep set economic and social problems leave Yilmaz little room for manoeuvre.
"In the West we talk about the 100 days' grace period for a new administration," said one foreign diplomat. "Given the scope of Turkey's problems, that may prove too generous."
